about: How an animal moves, by taxon (pipeline/locomotion.py resolves a species: every node from kingdom down to the species merges over the one above it, so a value is set once at the widest rank where it holds and overridden only where a narrower group differs; the numbers a species does not give are derived from its body by the allometric rules in locomotion.py, from mass_kg and size in its record). Units: m, m/s, s, rad/s. docs/movement.md explains the principles and which rank each belongs to.

Animalia.note: every animal: muscle shortens, so motion is a pull toward a point; mass sets the tempo (small is quick, large is slow); the body accelerates before it is drawn there (a lag), and nothing moves by itself: a limb or a fin pushes against the world and the body follows

Chordata.note: an axial skeleton: the head leads, the spine bends toward the turn, the tail trails; the body is bilateral and faces where it goes

Mammalia.note: limbs under the body (parasagittal), so the legs swing fore and aft and the gaits are walk, trot (or pace) and gallop, chosen by speed through the Froude number of the hip height (Alexander and Jayes 1983: walk to 0.5, trot to 2.5, gallop beyond); the spine flexes in the gallop; the head stays level over the stride; endotherm, so a sprint is aerobic for seconds to a minute by size
Mammalia.feet: turn by stepping: a standing turn walks in place, the fore feet toward the turn and the hind feet away, planted feet still on the ground

vary.note: strides that are never the same (docs/movement.md 'Strides that vary'; client/src/gait.js). Each number: what it is, then where it was read, or 'by eye' where no measurement was found. stride_cv [walk, trot, gallop]: the coefficient of variation of the stride interval within a bout. Trot 0.02: within one horse stride length and the durations of stride, stance and swing vary about 2 % at the trot (Drevemo, Dalin, Fredricson & Hjerten 1980, Equine Vet J 12:60-65, doi 10.1111/j.2042-3306.1980.tb02310.x); walk and gallop were not found: the walk a little wider and the gallop as the trot, by eye. drift: the weights of the stride clock's drift (a white part, then octaves 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 strides long), set so the stride intervals' DFA exponent sits near 0.87 +- 0.15, measured on people (Hausdorff et al. 1997, J Appl Physiol 82:262-269); no series from a quadruped was found. tempo_cv: an individual's own stride rate at a speed: between horses the same variables vary 2 to 3 times the 2 % within one (Drevemo et al. 1980), less the share its size already gives. size_cv, mass_cv: a coyote's mass varies 9-11 % within a sex and region (sd over mean: 16.4 +- 1.5, 14.7 +- 1.6, 12.1 +- 1.1, 10.6 +- 1.0 kg; Way 2007, Northeast Nat 14:111-124), so a length a third of that; mass_cv, the mass at a given size, by eye. phase_sd (a foot's landing against the diagram, of the stride), asym (an individual's left-right offset): by eye, inside what one dog shows between performances: the fore foot's timing 5 to 10 points of the stride (Hildebrand 1968, J Morphol 124:353-360). step_sd: a foot's reach, of the stride, kept small so stride length's spread stays near the 2 % (Drevemo et al. 1980). width_sd [fore, hind]: a foot's spread across, of the track's width: stance width varies 12.3 % (fore) and 5.9 % (hind) in mice on a treadmill (Amende et al. 2005, J NeuroEng Rehabil 2:20), a foot's share of it; none found for a dog, a horse or a deer. walk_lag (the fore foot's lag behind the hind of its side, slow walk to fast), pair_lag (the gallop's lag within a pair, slow to fast), shift (how much of a cycle a foot's lag may change in a stride): by eye; that the cycle changes continuously from walk to gallop in dogs is Maes et al. 2008 (J Exp Biol 211:138-149), whose numbers were not reached. lead.right: the share of individuals that lead with the right fore: 48.74 % of 2,095 racehorses (Cully et al. 2018, PLoS One 13:e0198545); lead.keep: dogs and pikas use their preferred trailing limb almost twice as often as the other, the preference the individual's (Hackert et al. 2008, Laterality 13:310-319); block (strides a choice lasts), hold_strides, turn_rad_s and the inside fore leading through a turn (riding practice; no measurement found): by eye. slope.hz: the stride rate's change per unit of slope (rise over run): galloping horses 2.01 to 2.08 strides a second on an 8-12 % incline (Parsons, Pfau & Wilson 2008, J Exp Biol 211:935-944), trotting horses 2.7 % slower on a 10 % decline (Hoyt, Wickler & Garcia 2006, Equine Vet J Suppl 36:573-579). soft.nod: the nose's range at the walk over the hip height, by eye here (hoofed walkers: Artiodactyla); the followers' rates (of stride_hz), damping and gains: by eye. square, stand_sd, foothold: by eye. excursion ([ahead at landing, behind at lift] degrees by gait: the most a standing leg's line from its shoulder or hip joint to the toe swings from the vertical; the engine's reach is the smaller of the leg's geometric reach and this angle's, a leg in the air swings no further than 1.1 (behind) and 1.15 (ahead) of it, and the walk's stride is capped so the legs' sweep covers its stance at a duty of 0.66, so a walk keeps a duty over a half): by eye. Searched for and not reached in figures: the touch-down and lift-off limb angles of trotting dogs (beagles at 1.4 m/s, the angle between the vertical and the line from the limb's fulcrum to its most distal marker: PMC5998594, whose numbers are in its figure and supplementary tables only) and of trotting horses (Sapone et al. 2021, Sensors 21:3792, read: canon-bone angles, given only as the biases of two IMU methods against motion capture). What was read: a horse trotting at 4 m/s stands 201.5 ms of a 641.5 ms stride, a duty of 0.31 (cited in Sapone et al. 2021); a galloping cheetah's swing can be as short as a greyhound's, 0.2 s, at stride frequencies up to 4 Hz (Hudson, Corr and Wilson 2012, J Exp Biol 215:2425, abstract), a duty near 0.2 at the top; the engine's gallop duties fall in that range limp: stride duration -2.05 % and the lame limb's duty factor +0.4 % at the walk under an induced lameness, the head's range at the trot up by half (Serra Braganca et al. 2021, Equine Vet J 53:600-611); the nod's size (rad at a limp of 1) by eye, its direction (down on the sound foot) from practice. Not in these numbers: a young animal. Its quicker steps follow from its size (dynamic similarity); foals change from walk to trot at the adults' Froude number but from trot to gallop at a lower one (Grossi & Canals 2010, J Exp Zool A 313:292-300), which the engine does not do.

idle.note: what a body that stands, feeds or lies keeps doing (client/src/idle.js; the engine's idle layer). Each number: what it is, then where it was read, or 'by eye'. breath.per_min_at_1kg and mass_exp: the resting breathing rate, 53.5 x mass_kg^-0.26 breaths a minute (Stahl 1967, J Appl Physiol 22:453; as converted from 0.89 M^-0.26 Hz quoted by Worthington et al. 1991, J Exp Biol 161:533; read from a search snippet, not the paper): a 13 kg coyote 27 a minute, a 230 kg elk 13. breath.cv (each breath's own length, a coefficient of variation), inhale (the share of a breath spent drawing in), chest ([across, in depth]: the chest's swell at the top of a breath, a share of its width and depth, about its own joint), spine (the spine's share of the chest's swell): by eye. breath.debt: after running the breath is quicker and deeper for a while: a debt filled toward the share of a gallop the body runs at over fill_s, paid back over tau_s_at_50kg x (mass/50)^mass_exp, the rate up by `rate` and the depth by `depth` at a full debt: all by eye (the mass exponent copied from the sprint's recovery, also by eye). weight: standing, the hips drift over one hind foot and back: shift (of a hind foot's distance from the midline), drop (the unloaded hip's fall, of the leg), roll (rad), hold_s ([median, sigma] of a log-normal hold), change_s (the shift's time), square (the share of holds square on both hind feet): by eye. look: the gaze: yaw (rad, the scan's reach either side; a caller's point may take 1.6 of it), pitch ([low, high] rad), ahead (the share of fixations straight ahead), hold_s ([median, sigma] of a fixation's hold, log-normal), turn_s_at_50kg and turn_exp (a turn's minimum-jerk time, from mass), neck (the neck's share of a turn, the head the rest), bed (the share of a turn a bedded body makes): by eye; no scan rates were found for these species, only that scanning falls as group size grows (Childress and Lung 2003, Anim Behav 66:389, elk; snippet), which the engine does not do. look.feed: feeding, the head comes up from the feed at intervals: every_s and up_s ([median, sigma], log-normal), rise_s: by eye. tail.style: the class's tail at rest is still (a family says otherwise). sit (on the haunches, the act's and a caller's): trunk_deg (the trunk's line from level, held below what the fore legs can stand to straight), seat (the hip joints' height above the ground, of their standing height): the hind feet step forward to lie flat beside the belly and the fore legs stand vertical under the shoulders; by eye. ears (a skeleton with ear joints): they point where the animal attends: swivel (rad, how far an ear turns about its base when it wanders), range (the most it turns), lead_s and lead_k (both turn toward the gaze's next fixation lead_s seconds before the head, by lead_k of the coming turn), hold_s ([median, sigma] of an ear's own log-normal hold when nothing holds the attention), turn_s (an ear's turn), back (the share of those holds turned out to its side or back), flick (per_min, s, amp rad: a quick small twitch), flat (rad back in the gallop and the shake), alert (rad forward and still in the alert), bed ([out, down] rad bedded), rest ([pitch, roll] rad, the carriage at rest): all by eye; no measured ear rates were found. gap_sigma: the sigma of the log-normal gap between acts; the gaps are log-normal because intervals between bouts of feeding in cattle are log-normal, not exponential (Tolkamp and Kyriazakis 1999, Anim Behav; snippet); the sigma by eye; the mean gap follows from the acts' shares. needs (an act's): what the skeleton must have for it to look right, tested once a skeleton (client/src/gait.js capsOf): neck_joints (at least so many joints in the neck), reach_neck (the engine's IK brings a hind toe within that share of the withers' height of its mark beside the neck); an act a skeleton cannot do leaves its repertoire and its share goes to standing, the shares here staying as nature has them; the thresholds by eye. acts: the repertoire, each with per_h (bouts an hour of standing) or share (of standing time; where a rank gives a share it wins over a wider rank's per_h) and bout_s ([median, sigma] of a log-normal bout). shake: the whole body twisted quickly from the head back along the spine and the tail at hz_at_1kg x mass^hz_exp: the exponent -0.22 is measured on 16 species of wet mammals, 0.01 to 260 kg, R2 0.95 (Dickerson, Mills and Hu 2012, J R Soc Interface 9:3208, abstract and text read); the prefactor (an image in the paper, not read) is set so a 30 kg Labrador shakes at its measured 4.5 Hz; a dry body's rate (per_h) and the bout by eye. sniff: the nose to the ground and along it, or (up: the share of sniffs) up into the wind: by eye. ruminate: false for the class (a ruminant's family says otherwise). Not drawn: the yawn, which needs a jaw (2.4 s in dogs and 1.97 s in cats: Gallup et al. 2016, Biol Lett 12:20160545, via the press)

Artiodactyla.note: unguligrade on hooves: a stiff-legged walk, a long trot, a bounding gallop; the alert is a frozen stance, head high

vary.note: the walk's nod: a horse's head moves 79 to 117 mm up and down at the walk, about 0.07 of its withers (Rhodin et al. 2022, Animals 12:3053); measured on horses (Perissodactyla), taken here for the hoofed walkers

idle.note: the hoofed: the tail switched in quick flicks at intervals (switch: every_s [median, sigma] log-normal, flicks [fewest, most] in a run, flick_s each, yaw rad): tail-switching rates rise with body mass across 26 bovids (Mooring et al. 2007, Biol J Linn Soc 91:383; snippet), but the per-species rates were not extractable, so the numbers are by eye and the same for every size. acts: the hind hoof's scratch at the neck (hz: its strokes a second) and the stamp (a fore foot lifted and set down hard), rates and bouts by eye. ruminate: bedded, the cud chewed at about 1 chew a second in runs of 34 to 46 chews, a bolus about 40 s (Pere David's deer: Li et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8:e66261, Table 2, read), a pause of 2 to 4 s between boli (cattle; snippet); the skeleton has no jaw yet, so it is drawn as the small nod the jaw's work gives the head (nod, rad: by eye), and it runs all the while the body is bedded (real rumination comes in bouts of tens of minutes: not modelled). Stated here for the ruminants (Ruminantia, a suborder the tree has no rank for); a non-ruminant family (the hippos, the pigs) says false. ears: the hoofed flick their ears more often, as they switch the tail (per_min, by eye)

Cervidae.note: the stot (all four feet off together) when alarmed, the white rump flag; a doe and a fawn walk in file

idle.note: the deer groom: mule deer groom 1 to 4 % of the day (Hudson and Kuzyk 2007, Can Field-Nat; snippet): here 2.5 % of standing time, 1.5 % the head round to the flank (groom: hz its licks a second) and 1 % the hind hoof's scratch; the day's share taken as standing time's, and the split and the bouts by eye; the deer's ears upright and mobile: a wider swivel, shorter holds (by eye). groom needs a neck of two or more joints (the head brought round to the flank: with one neck joint it turns in place like an owl's)

Carnivora.note: digitigrade (cats and dogs) or plantigrade (bears); a flexible spine that lengthens the gallop; the stalk, the rush and the pounce

idle.note: the hind foot's scratch at the neck or the ear (hz: strokes a second; the body half sits for it; needs reach_neck) and the sit on the haunches, held a long while (share of standing time, bout): by eye; sit: a dog or a wolf sits with its trunk at 45 to 50 degrees (trunk_deg 47, by eye)

Canidae.note: the trot is the travelling gait, hours long; the gallop is for the chase; the tail carries the mood. The catch is the mousing pounce: the prey fixed by ear with the head cocked, a frozen braced stance, a high stiff-legged spring onto it with the forelegs straight for the jar, the head down at the forepaws; the first pounce often misses and quick paw strikes follow; the kill is taken in the jaws with a head toss (docs/movement.md The catch)

feed.pose: the kill tossed in the jaws, then the nose down at it

idle.note: the tail carried low and still at rest (droop, rad below its carriage; a slow wag is a later, social lane); the bow (stretch); a third of sniffs up into the wind: by eye; ears upright and mobile: a wider swivel and shorter holds than the class's (by eye)

Felidae.note: a crouched stalk, then an explosive short rush of a few seconds and a pounce; a cat does not run far. The catch is the leap and the neck bite: the rush's last bound launches onto the prey's back, the forelegs reaching, the head driven into the nape or throat; over in seconds; then it feeds crouched over the kill, head low (docs/movement.md The catch)

catch.name: the leap and the neck bite

feed.pose: crouched over the kill, head low

idle.note: the tail's tip twitched at intervals (twitch: every_s [median, sigma] log-normal, twitch_s each, amp of the engine's twitch): by eye. groom: oral grooming is 4 % of a cat's time, 8 % of its time not resting (Eckstein and Hart 2000, Appl Anim Behav Sci 68:131; snippet): share 0.08 of standing time, sitting for it (sit), the head round to the shoulder or the flank, licking at hz a second (by eye); the bow (stretch): by eye; groom needs a neck of two or more joints. ears lower and rounder: carried a little down and out, a narrower swivel (by eye); sit: a cat sits more upright, 55 to 60 degrees (by eye)

Ursidae.note: plantigrade on the whole foot, an amble (a pace: the two legs of a side together) and a bounding run in bursts. The catch (not drawn yet) is the swat: a forepaw blow, then the bite

idle.note: a bear stands up into the wind to smell: two sniffs in five up (by eye); the tail too short to carry anything; ears small and nearly still: little swivel, little lead, rare flicks (by eye); sit: a bear sits more upright still, 60 to 70 degrees, the fore feet close to the hind (by eye)

Rodentia.note: the bound (the fore pair then the hind pair) at every speed above a walk, the sit-up on the haunches to look and to eat, a quick freeze; small, so the tempo is fast and the turns tight

Sciuridae.note: the tail flagged over the back, the bound with a long flight; the tree squirrels climb head-first down

Cricetidae.note: voles and mice: a scurry of quick short bounds close to the ground, runways through the grass

Lagomorpha.note: the half-bound hop: the long hind feet land together ahead of the fore feet; a standing turn pivots on the hind feet with hops of the fore feet; the freeze, then the burst and the zigzag

hop.note: client/src/gait.js hopStep: below shuffle_froude (of the hip height) the shuffle (the fore feet step one after the other, the hind pair hop up behind them); above it the half-bound (the fore feet land one after the other, the hind pair together ahead of them, a flight, the spine flexing and extending); the sit-up, the freeze and the form from the pose; the ears up when alert, laid back in flight or frozen

idle.note: the face wash (sitting up, the fore paws drawn down over the face, hz strokes a second) and the long hind foot's scratch at the neck: by eye; the hares' ears keep their own swivel (gait.js hopStep) and no gaze is drawn on them; no sniff (the nibble is the caller's flick); the ears' swivel (their wander by seed and clock drives the hares' own ear swivel, gait.js hopStep): wide (by eye); the scratch needs reach_neck

Lepus.note: the hares: a long lope on long hind legs, and every few bounds of it a higher, longer observation hop to look about

Reptilia.note: ectotherm: speed and endurance with the body's warmth, a sprint of a second or two then a rest; the sprawl

Squamata.note: sprawling limbs out to the side with the body low, and the body undulating side to side with the stride (the lateral wave); a turn is a C-bend of the whole body with the legs stepping round the sprawl; the push-up display

Aves.note: a biped on the ground: walk or hop, the head bobbing to hold the eyes still; the wings for flight: flap to climb, glide to settle, a stoop to dive; the head leads a turn on the neck

dive.note: every bird can close its wings and fall. The speed is a falling body's: weight along the slope against the drag of the tucked body, so it gains g sin(angle) less g (v / terminal)^2 and tends to terminal x sqrt(sin(angle)); terminal = sqrt(2 M g / (rho cd S_b)) with S_b the body's frontal area (pipeline/locomotion.py: Pennycuick's 0.00813 M^0.666 m^2, sea-level air), so it rises with mass^(1/6): a kinglet 31 m/s, a jay 48, a red-tail 74 in a vertical fall nobody has room for. cd 0.37 is the mean measured from the dives of small migrant passerines tracked by radar (Hedenstrom and Liechti 2001, J Exp Biol 204:1167; their range 0.17 to 0.77) and stands for every bird whose own is not measured. angle_deg 64 is the steepest dive track with a source here: a peregrine and a goshawk on tracking radar, 13 to 64 degrees, their fastest 10 s 31 to 39 m/s and about 30 m/s, well under terminal (Alerstam 1987, Ibis 129:267); no group's own steepest angle was found measured, so it stands for the class. A red-tail's 120 mph (54 m/s) and a golden eagle's 150 to 200 mph are repeated without a measurement behind them and are not used. pull_g_at_half_top: the spread wings at full lift slow a 1 kg model falcon at 1.5 g at half its top speed (Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:403), taken as the drag that sheds the dive's speed in the pull-out, as the square of the speed; modelled for a falcon, used for all. What keeps a jay's or a quail's drop short is the height it has, not a number here

Galliformes.note: runners first: a quick walk and a run with the head bobbing, a scratch and peck; flight is a burst flush of a few seconds and a glide downhill; no stoop of their own is recorded and none is given here: the class's fall applies, from the few metres a flush reaches

Passeriformes.note: hop on the ground, perch; flapping flight with glides between (the jays), or the raven's long cruising flight

Corvidae.note: walk as well as hop; the raven soars and tumbles. The catch is the bill stab: small prey (a lizard, a vole, a nestling) killed with repeated hard jabs of the bill at the head and chest until it is still; a jay dives, grabs in the bill and pecks; then it plucks and opens it with the bill (docs/movement.md The catch)

Accipitriformes.note: the soaring hawks: a slow flap, circling on thermals, a stoop

Accipitridae.note: the hawks' catch is the talon strike: from a perch or a stoop the wings fold and it drops, the legs and feet thrown forward at the last moment to grab, the kill by the talons piercing; then it mantles over the kill, wings half spread and drooped round it, head down (docs/movement.md The catch)

catch.name: the talon strike and the mantle

feed.pose: mantling: wings half spread and drooped round the kill, the tail fanned, head down

Falconidae.note: the falcons: the stoop, a long near-vertical dive with the wings closed to a teardrop, the strike in the air or at the ground

dive.note: cd 0.18 is the body drag measured on a peregrine at low speed, with which model falcons of 0.5 to 2 kg top out at 89 to 112 m/s in a vertical dive after about 1200 m (Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:403); a trained 1.02 kg gyrfalcon tracked optically dived at 17 to 62 degrees from up to 500 m (Tucker, Cade and Tucker 1998, J Exp Biol 201:2061; its fastest quoted second hand as about 58 m/s, the paper's own figure not read). angle_deg 87 has no tracked measurement behind it: the vertical stoop is the model's and the field descriptions', the tracked dives stop at 64 degrees; it is this game's limit for a stoop at prey since 2026-11-06

Cathartiformes.note: the vultures: teetering soar with the wings in a dihedral, rarely flapping

Piciformes.note: the woodpeckers: undulating flight (flap, close the wings, fall, flap), cling to the bark, hitch up it

species.note: a species names what no rank above it does: its size and mass (in its record), its own speeds where measured, its displays. Values here override the tree; the rest derive from the body.
